candidate_relations.reason: Normal echocardiography argues against cardiomyopathic dysfunction despite the preceding respiratory illness.
Rhinorrhea and sinus symptoms may precede the cardiac inflammation but do not explain troponin elevation.
Troponin I of 6.18 ng/mL supports myocardial injury, while the PR changes add required pericardial involvement.
The echocardiogram was normal and no stress-triggered regional ventricular abnormality was described.
A viral prodrome is suggestive but unproven, and this label omits the ECG-defined pericardial component.
Angiography showed normal coronary arteries while diffuse inferior ST and PR shifts favored inflammation.
Subjective fever and coryza were not accompanied by an influenza test or influenza-specific syndrome.
Preserved ventricular findings with classic pericarditic ECG changes favor myopericarditis rather than myocarditis-predominant perimyocarditis.
No apical ballooning or other wall-motion abnormality appeared on echocardiography.
ST elevation with PR depression supports pericarditis but does not account for marked troponin release.
The elevated troponin identifies myocardial inflammation only broadly and leaves the pericardial syndrome unspecified.
Jaw-radiating pressure, diaphoresis, inflammatory markers, and troponin elevation are not explained by costochondritis.
GERD would not produce PR-segment deviation or a troponin I level of 6.18 ng/mL.
Normal coronary angiography and pericarditic PR changes contradict an acute coronary mechanism.
Three hours of pressure could mimic spasm, but objective myocardial and pericardial inflammation cannot.
No hypoxemia, tachycardia, right-heart findings, or pulmonary imaging evidence supported embolism.
This label both omits myocardial injury and assigns an idiopathic cause despite a recent viral-like illness.
Dry cough and coryza can accompany bronchitis, but bronchitis does not explain the cardiac biomarkers and ECG.
A viral cause was not confirmed, and isolated viral pericarditis underrepresents the substantial troponin-defined myocarditis.
The patient had no pulse deficit, murmur, hemodynamic instability, or aortic imaging abnormality.
